NGM
NGM, The Social Planner problem: sequential form
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{The Planner’s Sequential Problem}}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\{c_t,i_t,n_t,k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}  
& \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t u(c_t) \qquad \quad \forall t = 0,1,2,\dots \\ 
\text{s.t.} \quad 
& c_t + i_t = F(k_t,n_t), 
&& \text{(Eq 1)} \\
& k_{t+1} = (1-\delta)k_t + i_t, 
&& \text{(Eq 2)} \\
& 0 \le n_t \le 1, 
&& \text{(Eq 3)} \\
& c_t \ge 0, \quad k_{t+1} \ge 0, 
&& \text{(Eq 4)} \\
& k_0 \ \text{given}, 
&& \text{(Eq 5)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
Note 1: since agents are identical, the planner’s problem can be written in terms of a \textcolor{red}{representative agent}.
Note 2: \textcolor{red}{u and F satisfy inada}, marginal utility when c / k / n is 0 is infinite, when c / k / n is infinite is 0. 

\bigskip

Reducing the Planner Problem: 
\begin{itemize}

\item \textcolor{blue}{Eliminate labor}: set to max, as it raises production but does not create disutility:\\ $n_t = 1$
\item \textcolor{blue}{Collapse constraints}
Take $i$ from equation 2, fill it in eq. 1. Rearranging:\[
c_t + k_{t+1} = \underbrace{F(k_t,1) + (1-\delta)k_t}_{f(k_t) \text{= total available resources}}
\qquad \text{(Eq 6)}
\]
If you include the non-negativity constraints: $$0 \le k_{t+1} \le f(k_t) \quad \forall t, \qquad \text{(Eq 7)}$$
\end{itemize}
The planner’s problem becomes\[
\max_{\{c_t,\, k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}} 
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t u(c_t)
\qquad \text{s.t.} \qquad
c_t + k_{t+1} = f(k_t) \quad \forall t,
\qquad
k_0 \text{ given.}
\]
(Equality constraint: Inada conditions guarantee $c_t > 0$, $k_{t+1} > 0$, so non-negativity never binds.)

At each date $t$, the decision is how to split available resources $f(k_t)$ between:
\begin{itemize}
    \item consumption today $c_t$, and
    \item capital carried into the next period $k_{t+1}$.
\end{itemize}

This is a \textcolor{red}{sequence problem}: the planner chooses entire infinite sequences $\{c_t, k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}$ that maximize lifetime utility, once and for all at time $0$.

nodes.title: Planner's Lagrangian: Basic NGM (deterministic, no labor)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Model 1: Basic NGM --- Deterministic, No Labor Disutility}}

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 0: Setup.}} Choices: $\{k_{t+1}\}$. State: $k_t$. No uncertainty, no labor choice ($n_t=1$).

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 1: Problem.}}
\[
\max_{\{k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t u\big(f(k_t) - k_{t+1}\big)
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
c_t + k_{t+1} = f(k_t),
\quad k_0 \text{ given.}
\]

\textcolor{red}{Convention (used throughout all models):} Inada conditions on $u$ and $f$ guarantee interior solutions ($c_t > 0$, $k_{t+1} > 0$). Non-negativity constraints never bind, so we write the resource constraint as an \textcolor{red}{equality} and use a single multiplier $\lambda_t \ge 0$. No complementary slackness conditions are needed.

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 2: Lagrangian.}}
\[
\mathcal{L}
=
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\beta^t
\Big[
u\big(f(k_t)-k_{t+1}\big)
+
\lambda_t
\big(
f(k_t) - k_{t+1} - c_t
\big)
\Big].
\]

\textcolor{red}{Convention:} $\lambda_t$ sits \emph{inside} the $\beta^t$ bracket (i.e.\ $\lambda_t$ is the \emph{current-value} multiplier). This convention is used in all models below.

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 3: FOCs.}}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] w.r.t.\ $c_t$: \quad $u'(c_t) = \lambda_t$
    \item[(ii)] w.r.t.\ $k_{t+1}$: \quad $\lambda_t = \beta \lambda_{t+1} f'(k_{t+1})$
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 4: Euler equation.}} Substitute (i) into (ii):
\[
\boxed{u'(c_t) = \beta\, u'(c_{t+1})\, f'(k_{t+1})}
\]
Interpretation: \textcolor{red}{MC} of saving one more unit (forgone consumption today) $=$ \textcolor{red}{MB} (discounted marginal utility tomorrow $\times$ marginal product of capital).

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 5: Boundary conditions.}}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $k_0$ given (initial condition).
    \item Finite horizon: $k_{T+1} = 0$.
    \item Infinite horizon: TVC $\lim_{t \to \infty} \beta^t u'(c_t) k_{t+1} = 0$ (discounted shadow value of capital vanishes).
\end{itemize}

\bigskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Solving: Log-Linearization Method}}

Analytically tractable only in simple cases (e.g.\ $u(c)=\ln c$, $f(k)=k^{\alpha}$, $\delta=1$). Otherwise, linearize around steady state:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Find steady state.
    \item Rewrite variables in log-deviations: $x_t = \bar{x}\, e^{\hat{x}_t}$.
    \item Substitute into the Euler equation.
    \item First-order Taylor expansion: $e^{z} \approx 1 + z$.
    \item Simplify using steady-state relations.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.title: Competitive equilibrium Problem
nodes.content:
Motivation:

- We have the planner result
- We now want the planner allocation to be \textcolor{red}{Decentralized}: can some system of prices $\exist$ st a system of households and firms reproduces the planner allocation?


Assume:
- households own (and supply) $l_t$ and capital stock $x_t$, make capital accumulation decisions
- Trade is sequential 
- Capital stock $x_t$ $\neq$ capital services $k_t$ supplied to firms. Capital services earn a rate. Capital depreciates at rate $\delta$, whether rented out or not. One unit of capital stock produces one unit of capital services; the constraint. $k_t \le x_t$ ensures the household cannot rent out more services than it owns.

nodes.title: Sequential form
Specify the Equilibrium condition
Decentralized CE: Basic NGM (deterministic, no labor)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Decentralized CE for Model 1 (Basic NGM): Same Template}}

\textbf{Goal:} Show that household + firm optimization reproduces the planner's allocation (Model 1).

\medskip
{\Large\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{Firm's Problem (static)}}}

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 1:}} $\max_{k_t,n_t}  F(k_t,n_t) - r_t k_t - w_t n_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 3 (FOCs):}} $F_k(k_t,n_t) = r_t$, \quad $F_n(k_t,n_t) = w_t$.

With CRS: $\pi_t = F - F_k k - F_n n = 0$ by Euler's theorem. Representative firm is WLOG.

\bigskip
{\Large\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{Household's Problem}}}

With $n_t = 1$, $k_t = x_t$, $\pi_t = 0$:

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 1: Problem.}}
\[
\max_{\{c_t,k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t u(c_t)
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
c_t + k_{t+1} = (r_t + 1-\delta)k_t + w_t,
\quad k_0 \text{ given.}
\]
Budget constraint as equality (Inada, same convention as planner problems).

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 2: Lagrangian.}}
\[
\mathcal{L} =
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\beta^t
\Big[
u(c_t)
+
\lambda_t \big( (r_t + 1 - \delta)k_t + w_t - k_{t+1} - c_t \big)
\Big].
\]
Same convention: $\lambda_t$ is current-value, inside $\beta^t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 3: FOCs.}}
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] w.r.t.\ $c_t$: \quad $u'(c_t) = \lambda_t$
    \item[(ii)] w.r.t.\ $k_{t+1}$: \quad $\lambda_t = \beta\, \lambda_{t+1}\, [r_{t+1} + 1-\delta]$
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 4: Euler equation.}} Substitute (i) into (ii), use $r_{t+1} = F_k(k_{t+1},1) = f'(k_{t+1}) - (1-\delta)$:
\[
\boxed{u'(c_t) = \beta\, u'(c_{t+1})\, f'(k_{t+1})}
\]
\textcolor{red}{Identical to the planner's Euler equation (Model 1).} Competitive prices decentralize the planner's allocation.

\textbf{\textcolor{orange}{Step 5: Boundary.}} $k_0$ given, TVC.

Planner's Lagrangian: Stochastic NGM (uncertainty, no labor)
Technology Process Governed by a Markov Process
nodes.content:
\section*{Technology Process Governed by a Markov Process}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Let the aggregate technology level $A_t(s^t)$ be a time-invariant function of last period’s level and the current shock $s_t$:
    
    \[
    A_t(s^t) = A\!\big(A_{t-1}(s^{t-1}),\, s_t\big).
    \]
    
    This means productivity evolves recursively: current productivity depends only on last period’s productivity and the current shock. The entire past history matters only through $A_{t-1}$ (Markov property).
    
   
    \item In recursive notation:
    
    \[
    A' = A s,
    \]
    
    where $A$ denotes current (past) productivity and $A'$ next period productivity. This compact form highlights the Markov structure: given $A$, only the current shock $s$ is needed to determine $A'$.
\end{itemize}

nodes.title: Recursive formulation
Time Invariant Markov Chains
nodes.content:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Assume $s_t$ follows a discrete-time, finite-state, time-invariant Markov chain.
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textcolor{red}{Markov property}: the next state depends only on the current state, not on the full past history.
        
        \item \textcolor{red}{Time invariance}: transition probabilities do not depend on time.
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\[
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s^t)
=
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s_t, s_{t-1}, \ldots, s_0)
=
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s_t).
\]

\bigskip

\begin{itemize}
    \item The Markov property implies:
\end{itemize}

\[
\pi(s^t)
=
\pi(s_t \mid s_{t-1})
\pi(s_{t-1} \mid s_{t-2})
\cdots
\pi(s_1 \mid s_0)
\pi_0(s_0),
\]

\[
\pi(s^t \mid s^\tau)
=
\pi(s_t \mid s_{t-1})
\pi(s_{t-1} \mid s_{t-2})
\cdots
\pi(s_{\tau+1} \mid s_\tau).
\]

how technology shocks drive wages in RBC models
nodes.content:
\textbf{1️⃣ What does a technology shock do?}

Production:
\[
Y_t = A_t F(K_t, N_t)
\]

If $A_t$ increases:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Output rises.
    \item The marginal product of labor rises.
    \item The marginal product of capital rises.
\end{itemize}

In competitive equilibrium:
\[
w_t = A_t F_n(K_t, N_t)
\]
\[
r_t = A_t F_k(K_t, N_t)
\]

Technology directly changes wages and returns.

\vspace{1em}

\textbf{2️⃣ Why are these ``intertemporal relative prices''?}

There are two key prices in this model:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] The wage $w_t$: price of leisure today.
    \item[(ii)] The return $r_{t+1}$: price of consumption tomorrow relative to today.
\end{itemize}

The Euler equation (Model 3):
\[
u_c(c_t, n_t) = \beta r_{t+1}\, u_c(c_{t+1}, n_{t+1})
\]

implies:
\[
r_{t+1}
=
\text{price of future consumption in units of today's consumption.}
\]

So:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Wage = intratemporal relative price (leisure vs.\ consumption today).
    \item Return = intertemporal relative price (today vs.\ tomorrow consumption).
\end{itemize}

\vspace{1em}

\textbf{3️⃣ What happens after a positive technology shock?}

Suppose $A_t$ increases temporarily.

Then:
\[
w_t \uparrow
\]
\[
r_t \uparrow
\]

This changes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item The price of leisure today (higher wage $\Rightarrow$ leisure more expensive).
    \item The price of consuming tomorrow (higher return $\Rightarrow$ future consumption more attractive).
\end{itemize}

Households therefore face new relative prices across time.

Rewrite in recursive form
nodes.content:
Start from the planner's sequential problem: 
\[
V(k_0) \equiv 
\max_{\{c_t,\, k_{t+1}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}}
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t u(c_t)
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad 
c_t + k_{t+1} = f(k_t) \quad \forall t,
\qquad
k_0 \text{ given.}
\]
Very important terminology: 
   \item $k_t$ is the \textcolor{red}{state variable}: it summarizes everything inherited from the past (Markov) and determines current feasible choices.

    \item $k_{T+1}$ is the \textcolor{red}{control variable}: it is chosen today and determines tomorrow’s state.
\end{itemize}


Separate current and future utility. Since $c_0 = f(k_0) - k_1$ from the resource constraint, rewrite as a nested maximization: 
\[
V(k_0)
=
\max_{c_0,\, k_1}
\left\{
u(c_0)
+
\beta\, V(k_1)
\right\}
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad c_0 + k_1 = f(k_0).
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item The crucial insight: the problem  is stationary, that is the problem faced tomorrow has the same structure as the problem faced today (preferences, technology, and constraints are time-invariant). A recursive formulation exploits stationarity to reduce it to a simpler problem.
    \item This recursive equation captures the planner’s \textcolor{red}{intertemporal trade-off}: more consumption today vs more (discounted) capital hence consumption tomorrow. 
\item What we achieved: the value function satisfies the bellman equation! This is a \textcolor{red}{functional equation}: the unknown object is the entire function V()! Does a solution exist, is it unique? and can we compute it? Y bc BE is a fp problem, and BE is a contraction under standard assumptions (recall contraction mapping theorem). Plus, CMT tells you that you that value function iteration converges to V, from any initial guess. We solve a single variable k' in each state k and get k' = g(k). By the otpimality principle, the sequeantially optimal path is the global optimal path.

nodes.title: Functional Euler Equation from Value Function Formulation
nodes.content:
\paragraph{Bellman Problem}
\[
V(k)
=
\max_{c,\, k'}
\Big\{
u(c) + \beta V(k')
\Big\}
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad c + k' = f(k).
\]
Define the objective (substituting $c = f(k) - k'$):
\[
\Phi(k,k') = u(f(k)-k') + \beta V(k').
\]
\bigskip
\paragraph{1. First-Order Condition (choice variable)}

Since the maximization is with respect to \( k' \),
\[
\frac{\partial \Phi(k,k')}{\partial k'}
= - u'(c) + \beta V'(k') = 0,
\]
where $c = f(k) - k'$. After solving, $k'$ becomes a function $k' = g(k)$ and $c = f(k) - g(k)$.


\bigskip
\paragraph{2. Envelope Condition}

Differentiate \( V(k) = \Phi(k,g(k)) \) with respect to \( k \). By the chain rule:
\[ V'(k) = \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial k} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial k'}}_{= 0 \text{ (FOC)}} g'(k) = \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial k}. \]
The FOC term vanishes (envelope theorem: $k'$ was already optimized). Hence:
\[
V'(k) = u'(c)\, f'(k).
\]

Substituting $V'(k') = u'(c')\, f'(k')$ into the FOC from Step 1:
\[
u'(c) = \beta\, u'(c')\, f'(k').
\]

\bigskip
\paragraph{3. Euler Equation}
Let $k_t = k,\; k_{t+1} = g(k),\; c_t = f(k_t) - k_{t+1},\; c_{t+1} = f(k_{t+1}) - k_{t+2}.$

\[
\boxed{
u'(c_t)
=
\beta\, u'(c_{t+1})\, f'(k_{t+1})
}
\]
Same Euler equation as Model 1 (Lagrangian approach).
